Issued at 422 AM CDT Sun Aug 23 2026

An upper level ridge axis extends from the Texas Panhandle 
through western North Dakota early this morning, with a 
shortwave ejecting off the Northern Rockies preceding a deeper 
closed low over western Washington. The shortwave will be the 
main focus for showers and thunderstorms developing in western 
and central North Dakota later this morning through this 
evening. A handful of models bring some weaker elevated 
convection into southwest North Dakota by mid morning, but 
there is better consensus for an increase in both coverage and 
intensity beginning in northwest North Dakota early this 
afternoon and spreading south and eastward through the late 
afternoon and evening hours. Showers and storms will develop 
over a boundary layer with a southerly, moisture-rich return 
flow, although there is some question whether an MCS over 
southwest South Dakota and northern Nebraska early this morning
could impede moisture transport to some extent. That uncertainty
aside, diurnal heating should contribute to CAPE increasing as 
high as 2000 J/kg with deep layer shear forecast to increase 
from 30 kts in the afternoon to 40 kts in the evening. There 
are some factors that could dampen the intensity of convection, 
including mid level lapse rates less than 6 C/km and a capping 
inversion that boundary layer mixing and cooling aloft from 
height falls may not be able to fully erode. Nevertheless, 
recent CAMs have certainly honed in on an outcome that includes
a few severe thunderstorms over parts of western and central 
North Dakota from mid afternoon through this evening. A lack of
a well-defined surface boundary and a mixture of shear and deep
layer wind vector orientation to the dewpoint/CAPE gradient 
would seemingly point toward a multicell/cluster storm mode, 
which fits with CAMs' reflectivity simulations. Confidence in 
sustained supercellular structure is low, so have limited our 
most likely maximum hail size forecast to ping pong balls for 
now. If upscale growth can lead to more organized convection, 
damaging winds up to 70 mph could emerge as the dominant severe 
hazard, especially in the evening when 0-3 km shear could 
increase to 35 kts. Despite low LCLs and 0-1 km shear greater 
than 10 kts, model hodographs do not appear to be supportive of
tornadogenesis. While instantaneous rainfall rates could be 
quite high with these storms, their forward propagation should 
limit the risk for localized flooding, with urban areas being a
possible exception. 

Back to the west, the deeper closed low is forecast to eject 
off the Canadian Rockies this evening. Lee cyclogenesis is 
already underway from Alberta through central Montana, but the 
lee trough/cold front is not forecast to reach western North 
Dakota until later tonight. Models have shown mixed signals on 
whether strong to severe convection associated with the trough 
in central/eastern Montana this afternoon and evening will 
survive into western North Dakota later tonight. More recent 
guidance has trended to a lower probability of convective 
maintenance, which may be due in part to the increased 
probabilities of thunderstorms in North Dakota stabilizing the 
air mass in between the two convective systems. MUCAPE is 
actually projected to remain as high as 2000 J/kg through the 
night in western North Dakota, but model soundings reveal the 
most-unstable layer to be highly-capped. Depending on the 
timing of decaying convection, there could be some higher wind 
gusts sneaking across the Montana border around midnight.

A conditional threat for severe storms continues in central and
eastern North Dakota on Monday, but confidence in convective 
initiation is quite low. Even though several forcing mechanisms 
are forecast to be present, including mid level height falls/ 
DCVA, low level warm air convergence, and surface convergence 
along the frontal boundary attendant to the Canadian low, there 
may not be enough of an alignment of these features to ensure 
deep moist convection initiates, and there are a number of 
possible scenarios and combinations thereof being displayed by 
the suite of CAMs. First, there is potential for elevated 
morning convection moving across northern North Dakota ahead of 
the surface front in an area where stronger warm air advection 
on the mesoscale could overlap with stronger height falls as 
the Canadian upper low spins over southern Saskatchewan. This 
may or may not play a role in afternoon convection if it 
occurs. A capping inversion will almost certainly delay 
surface-based convection until late afternoon and early 
evening. Then it becomes a question of whether strong enough 
forcing will come into alignment for sustained deep moist
